title: LLVM Optimizations
concept: LLVM applies dozens of optimization passes to your IR — inlining, dead code elimination, constant folding, and more. Understanding them explains XIOM's performance.
why: XIOM doesn't need to implement every optimization. LLVM provides battle-tested passes that transform naive IR into highly optimized machine code. Knowing what LLVM does explains why your code is fast.
theory:
## LLVM's Optimization Pipeline

### Major Optimization Passes

```sh
# View which passes LLVM applies
xiom build --emit-ir --verbose 2>&1 | grep "Pass:"
```

### 1. Inlining

```llvm
; Before inlining:
define i64 @square(i64 %x) {
  %sq = mul i64 %x, %x
  ret i64 %sq
}
define i64 @main() {
  %r = call i64 @square(i64 5)
  ret i64 %r
}

; After inlining:
define i64 @main() {
  %sq = mul i64 5, 5
  ret i64 %sq
}
```

### 2. Constant Folding

```llvm
; Before:
%a = add i64 2, 3
%b = mul i64 %a, 10

; After constant folding:
%a = i64 5   ; 2 + 3 = 5
%b = i64 50  ; 5 * 10 = 50
```

### 3. Dead Code Elimination (DCE)

```llvm
; Before:
%x = call i64 @expensive()
ret i64 42

; After DCE (x is never used):
ret i64 42
```

### 4. Loop Optimizations

| Optimization | What It Does |
|-------------|-------------|
| Loop unrolling | Duplicate loop body N times |
| Loop invariant hoisting | Move constant computation out of loop |
| Loop vectorization | Use SIMD for parallel iterations |
| Loop fusion | Combine consecutive loops |
| Loop fission | Split complex loops |

### 5. Common Subexpression Elimination (CSE)

```llvm
; Before:
%t1 = mul i64 %a, %b
%t2 = add i64 %t1, %c
%t3 = mul i64 %a, %b   ; Same as t1!
%t4 = sub i64 %t3, %c

; After CSE:
%t1 = mul i64 %a, %b
%t2 = add i64 %t1, %c
%t4 = sub i64 %t1, %c  ; Reuses t1
```

### Optimization Levels

| Level | Passes | Compile Speed | Runtime Speed |
|-------|--------|---------------|---------------|
| O0 | None | Fastest | Slowest |
| O1 | Basic (inlining, CSE) | Fast | Faster |
| O2 | Standard (loop opts, GVN) | Medium | Fast |
| O3 | Aggressive (vectorization) | Slow | Fastest |
| Os | Size-focused | Medium | Fast |
| Oz | Size-aggressive | Slow | Medium |
syntax_ref:
# Control optimization level:
xiom build -O0 main.xi    # No optimization
xiom build -O2 main.xi    # Standard optimization
xiom build -O3 main.xi    # Aggressive optimization

# View optimization passes:
xiom build --emit-ir --verbose main.xi
tips: Trust the optimizer for micro-optimizations — write clear code, let LLVM make it fast
Constant folding eliminates compile-time-known computations — use const for intentional constants
Inlining is the gateway optimization — it enables other optimizations by exposing more context
Write small, pure functions — they inline better and enable more optimization opportunities
common_mistakes: Trying to outsmart the optimizer — 'clever' code often prevents optimizations
Assuming -O3 always produces faster code than -O2 — sometimes bigger code is slower (cache effects)
Forgetting that debug builds (-O0) don't optimize at all — contracts and overflow checks add overhead
